name: South Korea
summary: South Korea taxes residents on worldwide income. Gains on foreign shares cost 22%, while Korean listed shares are exempt below major-shareholder thresholds. Financial income above KRW 20 million a year is taxed at up to 49.5%. Foreigners resident five years or less in ten are taxed on foreign dividends only if they are remitted to Korea. Inheritance tax is estate-based at 10%-50%, with a KRW 500 million deduction, and covers worldwide assets of a resident. There is no net wealth tax, but a national holding tax on high-value housing applies. An exit tax reaches foreign shares from 2027.

regimes.name: Korean resident (worldwide)
regimes.description: Worldwide taxation: foreign-share gains 22%, financial income above KRW 20 million at up to 49.5%; estate-basis inheritance tax up to 50%.
regimes.eligibility: Resident if domiciled in Korea or residing 183 days or more in a tax year (from 2026 also 183 consecutive days spanning two years). Foreigners are taxed worldwide once resident more than five of the last ten years.

capital_gains.summary: Capital gains are taxed separately from global income. Gains on Korean listed shares are exempt for shareholders below the 'major shareholder' thresholds (1% stake on KOSPI, or KRW 5 billion market value). Gains on foreign shares are taxed at 20% national plus 10% local income tax (22% in total) after a KRW 2.5 million annual deduction. Major shareholders' Korean shares and unlisted shares are taxed at 22% up to KRW 300 million of gain and 27.5% above (local tax included). Real estate gains are taxed at the progressive rates of 6%-45% plus local tax, with a long-term holding deduction.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: KRW 2.5 million basic deduction per category per year. One house per household exempt under conditions (high-value homes partly taxable).
capital_gains.important_exceptions: The planned financial investment income tax was repealed before taking effect (general knowledge). Exit tax: residents of 5+ years who are major shareholders pay tax on unrealised gains on Korean shares when emigrating; from 1 January 2027 foreign shares are included (above KRW 500 million in total, with carve-outs for foreign employees). Heavier rates for multi-home owners in regulated areas have been suspended by decree (status after May 2026 not verified).

capital_gains.rate_basis: Foreign listed shares 20% + 10% local = 22%. Domestic listed 0 for a holding below 1% and KRW 5 billion. Private business (unlisted, major shareholder) 25% + local = 27.5% on gains above KRW 300 million. Real estate: top 45% + local = 49.5% before the long-term holding deduction (up to 30% of the gain for general property held 15 years; more for a qualifying single home). Foreign real estate taxed the same way once resident 5 years.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Trading as a business is business income at global rates up to 49.5%.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: Major-shareholder shares held under one year: 33%. Real estate held under 1-2 years: higher flat rates (not detailed).
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Foreign shares are taxed to any resident at 20% national + 2% local (Income Tax Act art. 94(1)(iii)(c), art. 104; NTS guide), after the KRW 2.5 million deduction shared with Korean shares. Gains on foreign assets other than shares are taxable only if the seller has been resident 5 years or more at the time of sale (PwC). Foreign-share gains taxed at 22%.

dividends.summary: Dividends are part of financial income: up to KRW 20 million a year is taxed at 15.4% (14% plus local tax) by withholding; above that, financial income is added to global income at progressive rates up to 45% plus 10% local tax (49.5%). Domestic dividends get a gross-up and dividend tax credit. Foreign dividends of residents taxed on worldwide income are included at global rates with a foreign tax credit. From 2026 to 2028, dividends from qualifying high-dividend Korean companies can be taxed separately at 14%-30%.
dividends.important_exceptions: Foreign residents with five years or less of residence in the last ten are taxed on foreign dividends only if paid by a Korean entity or remitted to Korea (special regime).

dividends.rate_basis: Foreign: 45% + 10% local = 49.5% before credit. Domestic: grossed-up dividend (10% gross-up, Income Tax Act art. 17(3)) taxed at 45% less a credit equal to the gross-up gives 39.5% national + 3.95% local = 43.45%; the credit equals the gross-up amount (art. 56); qualifying high-dividend companies 2026-2028: separate 14%-30% national.
dividends.withholding_outbound: 22% WHT (20% + local) on dividends to non-residents, reducible by treaty (not opened).
dividends.treaty_network: 97 income tax treaties as of January 2026, including the US and EU states (PwC).
dividends.holding_company_notes: CIT 10%-25% plus local tax; dividends received deduction for Korean subsidiaries (not researched).

wealth_tax.summary: No net wealth tax (PwC). Korea does levy a national comprehensive real estate holding tax (CRET, 종합부동산세) on individuals whose total official value of housing exceeds KRW 900 million (KRW 1.2 billion for a one-house household); it is treated here as a property tax, not a wealth tax, because it reaches only Korean real estate and its current rate schedule could not be verified.

sources.title: Korea, Republic of - Individual - Other taxes
종합부동산세 (Comprehensive real estate holding tax)

open_questions: CRET is arguably a limited wealth tax on Korean housing; it was not modelled because the 2026 brackets were not verified.
wealth_tax.property_tax_note: Local property tax 0.07%-5% of statutory value (PwC). CRET (national): on (official housing value - KRW 900 million / 1.2 billion) x fair-market-value ratio, progressive rates (top 2.7% for owners of two homes or fewer and up to 5% for three or more under the 2023 law, from general knowledge, not verified), plus 20% rural special tax. A EUR 5 million home would pay CRET. Acquisition tax 1%-12%.

inheritance.summary: Korea levies inheritance tax on the whole estate (estate basis) at 10%-50%: 10% up to KRW 100 million, 20% to 500 million, 30% to 1 billion, 40% to 3 billion and 50% above. A lump-sum deduction of KRW 500 million (or a basic deduction plus personal deductions) and a spouse deduction of at least KRW 500 million (up to 3 billion) apply. Gift tax uses the same rates per recipient, with a deduction for gifts from parents to an adult child of KRW 50 million per 10 years (KRW 20 million for a minor). Gifts within 10 years before death are added back to the estate.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: Lump-sum deduction KRW 500 million per estate: the larger of KRW 500 million and the basic deduction (KRW 200 million, art. 18) plus personal deductions (KRW 50 million per child, art. 20), art. 21; for three adult children the second is KRW 350 million, so KRW 500 million applies. Spouse deduction KRW 0.5-3 billion (art. 19). Financial-asset deduction: 20% of net financial assets (at least KRW 20 million, at most KRW 200 million; art. 22), excluding shares held by a largest shareholder; whether a portfolio in foreign custody counts as a financial asset 'handled by a financial company' (Decree art. 19) was not established, so it is not coded. 3% credit on the computed tax for filing on time (art. 69), not coded.
inheritance.important_exceptions: Government proposals (heir-based taxation, a higher child deduction, a top rate of 40%) were not enacted: the 2024 bill was rejected in December 2024 and the heir-based system is 'under government review' for about 2028 (koreainheritance.com guide, mid-2026); the Act text current to 2026-01-02 still has the estate-based scale. Business succession deduction for family businesses does not cover a listed portfolio. A controlling shareholder's unlisted shares are valued 20% higher (art. 63(3)).

inheritance.business_relief: Family business succession deduction (up to KRW 60 billion) for qualifying SMEs and mid-sized companies; not for portfolio shares.
inheritance.foreign_assets: If the deceased was a Korean resident (domicile or residence of 183 days or more), worldwide assets are taxed; for a non-resident deceased, Korean assets only.
inheritance.domicile_rules: Residence of the deceased decides scope; there is no special exclusion for foreign nationals (not verified). Gift tax: a resident recipient is taxed on worldwide gifts.

dividends.rate_basis: Foreign dividends 0 if kept abroad (remittance basis); domestic as standard.
dividends.eligibility_conditions: Remittance basis: the 0% foreign_gross_rate ASSUMES foreign dividends are paid and kept abroad. Dividends paid by a Korean company, or foreign dividends paid in Korea or remitted to Korea, are taxed in full (Income Tax Act art. 3(1) proviso).

capital_gains.summary: A foreign national with 5 years or less of residence in the last 10 is taxed on foreign-source income only if it is paid in Korea or remitted to Korea (Income Tax Act art. 3(1) proviso; the text covers all income, gains included). Gains on foreign shares sold through a foreign broker, with the proceeds kept abroad, are therefore outside the charge; shares sold through a Korean broker, or proceeds remitted to Korea, are taxed as in the standard regime (22%). Korean listed shares and unlisted shares as standard. Gains on foreign assets other than shares are taxable only after 5 years of residence (PwC).
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Same KRW 2.5 million deduction as the standard regime for gains that are taxed.
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: Remittance basis: the 0% rate for foreign shares and foreign real estate ASSUMES the proceeds are paid and kept abroad. Anything remitted to Korea, or paid by a Korean broker or bank, is taxed. The statute has no ordering rule for remittances, so the family's living costs paid from abroad into Korea can pull gains into the charge.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Same as the standard regime for exit tax and Korean-source gains.

capital_gains.foreign_assets: Foreign-source gains taxed only if paid in or remitted to Korea during the first 5 years (more than 5 years in the last 10: worldwide).

regimes.name: Family investment company (Korean stock company, jushik hoesa)
regimes.description: The family holds the portfolio through a Korean stock company owned by the parents. The company pays corporate income tax on its worldwide income at 10% to KRW 200 million, 20% to KRW 20 billion, 22% to KRW 300 billion and 25% above (fiscal years from 1 January 2026), plus local income tax of 1%/2%/2.2%/2.5% on the same bands; the reference family's profit (about KRW 1.5 billion) is in the 20% + 2% = 22% band at the margin. Portfolio dividends and gains are fully taxable (no exclusion below a 10% stake for foreign dividends; 30% exclusion for Korean dividends on stakes under 20%). Foreign withholding is credited against the national tax, and the local tax base is reduced by the foreign tax. Distributions to the parents are financial income at up to 49.5% less the dividend credit (43.45%). Inheritance tax is as for direct holding, so that metric is inherited from the standard regime.
regimes.eligibility: Any person may found a stock company under the Commercial Act (no minimum capital; not verified) and hold its shares; a foreign national who also directs it needs a residence status that permits it (not verified). Selling existing foreign shares to the company is a taxable disposal for the individual (22% on the gain), so the model assumes the company is funded with cash or shares at current cost.
regimes.duration_note: A company under ordinary law with no time limit. Its tax position changes only with the corporate rate schedule (raised by one point in every band from 1 January 2026).

structure.entity: Family investment company (Korean stock company) held by the parents
structure.payout_notes: Dividends paid to a resident individual are financial income: 14% withholding (15.4% with local tax) up to KRW 20 million of financial income a year, above that added to global income at up to 45% + 4.5% local. Dividends of a Korean company are grossed up by 10% and a credit equal to the gross-up applies (Income Tax Act arts. 17(3), 56): 1.1 x 45% - 10% = 39.5% national + 3.95% local = 43.45%. The dividend credit is not given on dividends paid out of income that was not taxed at the company, which does not apply here. Salary to a director would be deductible for the company but needs real work.
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: Korean-resident company, so no controlled-foreign-company issue for foreign holdings held through it. Not researched: gift-tax rules on benefits conferred through transactions with a closely held company, and the treatment of companies whose main business is investment (no SME status). The 20% additional tax on excess retained earnings applies only to large conglomerate companies until 2028 (PwC).
structure.exit_and_liquidation: Liquidation distributions above paid-in capital are deemed dividends (financial income, art. 17(2)). Emigration of the parents triggers the exit tax on Korean and, from 1 January 2027, foreign shares of major shareholders (see standard regime), including the company's shares if unlisted; not analysed. At death the shares form part of the estate; unlisted shares of a company whose assets are mostly shares are valued at net asset value, and a controlling shareholder's shares carry a 20% valuation premium unless the company is an SME or mid-sized company (art. 63(3)).

The 10%/1% band on the first KRW 200 million, and the foreign-tax reduction of the local tax base, are ignored (the model uses a single rate). Real estate held in the company would also bear a surtax on land gains (Corporation Tax Act art. 55-2, not researched); not modelled.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Not relevant: all company income is taxable profit.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Worldwide profits taxed; foreign tax credit with a ten-year carry-forward (PwC).

dividends.summary: Portfolio dividends received by the company are taxable income at 22% at the margin. Foreign dividends from stakes under 10% get no 95% exclusion, and the foreign tax credit is then available (PwC). Korean dividends on stakes under 20% are 30% excluded, so 70% is taxed. Foreign tax is credited against the national tax within the limit and deducted from the local tax base (Local Tax Act art. 103-19(2)).
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: Domestic dividends: 100% excluded at 50% or more ownership, 80% at 20%-50%, 30% below 20% (from 1 January 2023, PwC). Foreign dividends: 95% excluded at a 10% stake or more (not for the family's portfolio holdings).
